newsitem.title: JAPAN: N.Korea says would not go to war over food crisis.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea says would not go to war over food crisis.

text.p: Famine-threatened North Korea said on Thursday it would not go to war to resolve a food crisis which it said had reached a "serious stage".

But Pyongyang warned that its patience was running out, with the United States and its allies using the crisis to portray North Korea as a nation poised to launch an attack to divert the attention of its people from the famine.

A spokesman for North Korea's Foreign Ministry, in a report carried by the official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), said even its 1.1 million strong military was involved in the battle to head off starvation after two consecutive years of flooding.

"it is true our temporary food shortage has reached a serious stage," he said. "Our arable lands have been severely devastated and agricultural output drastically decreased owing to natural disasters which have been repeated in recent years when the economic blockade of the hostile forces has been further tightened.
"But war is not what we want," the spokesman added.
The no-war assurance comes at a time when speculation is rife that hunger-stricken North Korea could opt for war against its arch-enemy, capitalist South Korea.
A recent North Korean defector said in Seoul on Thursday that Pyongyang had tested its preparedness to launch military attacks on the South in March.

In Manila on Wednesday, Admiral Joseph Prueher, commander-in-chief of U.S. forces in the Pacific, warned that forcing North Korea into a corner could drive it to attack its southern neighbour, resulting in heavy loss of life.
International aid agencies have warned that tens of thousands of people could starve to death over the next few months unless substantial food aid is sent to North Korea.
The United Nations' World Food Programme (WFP) estimates that North Korea needs 1.3 million tonnes of food to meet basic needs in 1997. It has appealed for 200,000 tonnes of food.
But pledges of aid have been slow due to scepticism about how bad the situation is in North Korea and whether food aid would be used mainly to feed North Korea's powerful military.

George Weber, secretary-general of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), told a news conference in Seoul on Thursday that North Korea was desperately short of food, but not yet starving.
"We're in a pre-famine situation. We do not have a famine yet," he said. "We cannot confirm, as of today...that thousands are dying."
The North Korean spokesman said Pyongyang had been "frank" in informing the international community of its plight.
"Moreover, we have mobilised even servicemen to do farming to surmount the difficulties with our own efforts," he said.
He accused Washington, Seoul and Tokyo of trying to use food aid as a "political weapon".
Washington has made clear that once peace talks start, stepped up aid is a strong possibility.
North Korea last month agreed to join proposed four-nation peace talks if it was first guaranteed large-scale food aid, U.S. diplomatic recognition and an easing of trade sanctions.
Peace talks involving the two Koreas, the United States and China would be aimed at closing the book on the 1950-53 Korean War, which ended in a now-fraying armistice.
"With North Korea refusing to comply with their political demand, they (the U.S., Japan and South Korea) are now raising a hue and cry over a 'possible war'," the North Korean spokesman said.
"The present situation, therefore, makes us more keenly feel that it is necessary to sharpen vigilance and increase the defence capabilities of the country as never before."
